A press dispatch from Hamilton,

Haythorne, an official of the national selective service, Ottawa, on Monday last told the annual meeting of the Canadian Political Science association that 60,000 additional farm workers, without making allowance for farmers who have joined the armed forces, are needed to obtain the extra quantities of farm products required for the current year. house will realize that the movement of coal miners from any industry must proceed in conformity with the terms of the order in council recently passed after consultation with labour organizations and employers. It should be pointed out that some criticism has been expressed by hon. members of this house with respect to the principle of compulsory transfer, in that the government has not gone far enough in this regard. I need hardly repeat that a grave emergency confronts the country so far as the coal supply is concerned, and of course coal mining in itself is an important basic industry, particularly in this country where we are on an import rather than an export basis. Without coal we cannot have ships, and it is essential that all members of the House of Commons lend their support to the government to face up to the fuel problem that confronts us at the present

Mr. Speaker, I sent notice to the
Minister of Labour of a question similar to the one asked by the hon. member for North BattLeford (Mrs. Nielsen). What machinery is being provided for the moving of employees from other war industries back to mining? At the plant in question .there are 200 miners who were specially trained in shipbuilding. But many of those men are not physically able to return to the occupation of coal mining. If they are to be moved en bloc the net result will be a good deal of unemployment, and this will affect men who are now doing an essential service. maintopic: TRANSFER OF COAL MINERS FROM SHIPBUILDING PLANTS
speechtext:
I am sure the hon. member will appreciate the difficulties faced' by national selective service. In the course of the last two weeks I have listened to many speeches in the house respecting the principle of selective service. It has been suggested that we are not moving with expedition. I said a year ago, when this responsibility was placed upon my shoulders, that you had asked for total war and you would get it. In connection with any development there must be sufficient machinery1 to do the work. One cannot overload a machine, or load it to capacity until it is incapable of taking care of the tremendous load placed upon it. My hon. friend can rest assured that selective service will use common sense and good judgment in the moving of men and women from one industry to another.
I know the difficulties confronted by hon. members, and I am sure they appreciate mine, particularly when we have to uproot people and put them into a basic industry, where they are absolutely necessary. May I repeat that coal mining-and I speak for myself- is infinitely more important in this country at the present time than shipbuilding. Perhaps the hon. member is more familiar than I am with the coal mining industry. He knows the climate of this country as well as I do, and will realize that it is far better to take these precautions now than to wait until next fall, and then be faced with the kind of emergency with which I was faced in the western provinces at a time when the temperature was down to forty-two degrees below zero, and the people did not have enough coal for the following day.

I repeat that I think it is the duty of all of us, when dealing with these 'basic industries, to lend every possible support to the government and to face up to our difficulties.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROCEDURE IN OBTAINING APPLICATION AND RENEWAL FORMS
speechtext: Yesterday the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lockhart) raised a question about the distribution of passport application forms, and said at the time that he did not attach much importance to the waste of paper that was involved.

subtopic: PROCEDURE IN OBTAINING APPLICATION AND RENEWAL FORMS
speechtext: Not in view of the way it is circulated around this House of Commons; divorce bills and the like.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROCEDURE IN OBTAINING APPLICATION AND RENEWAL FORMS
speechtext:
The Department of External Affairs is trying to set an example to the other branches of the government.
In reply to the hon. member I would say it has been found that the old practice _ of sending bulk supplies of blank application forms to post offices, railway ticket offices, banks, law firms and travel agencies across the country for the use of potential applicants resulted in the waste of hundreds of thousands of application forms which were never used. Such a practice, while a convenience for the public and justifiable under the easy conditions of peace, would, it is felt, be unnecessary as well as wasteful under conditions of war, when the demand for passports is greatly reduced. It seems doubtful also whether it *is a sound practice for transportation companies and other interested parties to fill out application forms for passport applicants. For the information of hon. members I may say that the government of the United States requires applicants to apply on their own behalf for application forms and charges a fee of $1 for each blank application form.

Under the new arrangement application forms are kept in stock at the passport office, Ottawa, and will be available on the personal application or written request of the person desiring to apply for a passport or a renewal. An exception is made, however, in the case of companies who desire to send any considerable number of employees to the United States, provided they indicate the actual number of employees they are sending for whom passports are required. There should not be any real trouble or delay in having applicants write in for an application or a renewal form. For short trips to the United. States passports are no longer required. Longer trips under war conditions require extensive preparations and consequently there is ample time for applicants to secure an application form and a passport. If stocks of passport application and renewal forms are made available at some points, as the hon. member suggests, in fairness they woidd have to be made available right across the country. The result would be a return to the old system which, as I have said, was found to be somewhat wasteful.

subtopic: PROCEDURE IN OBTAINING APPLICATION AND RENEWAL FORMS
speechtext: I suggested yesterday that the post office might be the medium through which this could be done. I do not see why that would not be possible, because every postmaster is a civil servant in the employ of the government of Canada. Emergencies do arise when people require passports, and it takes time to write to Ottawa and get the necessary form. It seems to me the post office should be a satisfactory medium through which to issue these forms.

speechtext: The house resumed from Tuesday, May 25, consideration in committee of a resolution to grant to his majesty certain sums of money for the carrying out of measures consequent upon the existence of a state of war-Mr. Ilsley-Mr. Bradette in the chair.
Pay and allowances, $539,730,211.

Mr. Chairman, the
government is again asking the house to vote an enormous sum of money, almost four billions of dollars, for the prosecution of the war. Before Canada's participation in the war her unemployed population lived on direct relief, or public charity. There was no money available for construction projects, but there is plenty available now to kill and destroy. It is a frightful race toward the abyss. Some might say the country had never known such prosperity, and that never before have so many people worked in factories. This is true. But what wastage of materials, money and working hours do we not see!
Go into war factories and see for yourselves the output of those industries. One would be stunned by what he would see. Workers who are only too willing to work for their salaries are condemned to idleness, because of the lack of material and poor administration of the factories. Scandals unearthed in war factories, where pay lists were tampered with and swollen, as was the case recently in Montreal, constitute a condemnation of the war policy of the government.
Some company presidents had their salaries increased from $10,000 to $30,000. These shameful war profiteers completed their treason by entering fictitious names on their workers' lists. The government discovered these shameful abuses only after two years of speculation and robbery. Has not the administration any competent accountants and auditors who could supervise the operations of these factories? Why has fraud, wastage and robbery prevailed in those factories for many months, and even years? While the first necessities of life are being rationed to the defenders of the country and to the civilian population, why were soldiers' food and woollen blankets stolen from' certain camps? Will the government ever take steps, once and for all, to stop this deplorable state of affairs? When will it appoint experienced cooks to prepare all the food in training camps? Who can estimate the enormous quantities of meat, eggs, vegetables and bread which are wasted in the camps because of the ignorance and incompetence of the cooks? We are receiving complaints of . this type every day. These are not isolated cases. This seems to be general everywhere. The government are asking the farmer to provide the utmost production, and yet they deprive him of his best help. Requests have been made from time to time that the department concerned should send back to the farms the experienced farmers who have been called to the colours and are still in the armed forces. But nothing has beeD done. There is nothing extraordinary in this attitude; the administration seems to persist in continuing its stupid inconsistencies. On the one hand it advocates increased agricultural production, yet on the other hand it pays the prairie farmer to reduce his production. Such methods call for restrictions of all kinds. We have them.
Are our leaders satisfied with this work? The disastrous policy of the government is responsible for the rationing we now have in Canada. This is the main reason for the increase in the cost of living. Why must this untruthful propaganda which we hear every day over the radio be continued? Who will believe that in the last three months the price of meat, food and clothing has gone up only 1-8 per cent?
War Appropriation-Army

I have here a release by the wartime prices and trade board which was published in the Montreal La Presse on April 30, 1943. A translation reads:
The Price of Beef is Increased
The wartime prices and trade board to-day announces its official chart of maximum prices -a prelude to the coming rationing of meat.
In order to prepare for the rationing of meat and to protect consumers, the foods division of the wartime prices and trade board has just prepared a chart of the different cuts of beef authorized for sale and a list of the maximum prices for the districts of Montreal, Quebec, Ottawa and Hull. These prices are to be effective to-day.
The Montreal district includes a zone which covers a radius of twenty-five miles from the city hall. In all butchers' stores or wherever beef is sold to consumers, this list must be posted in a place where the public can easily read it or refer to it when the need arises.
Consumers will be protecting themselves and acting in their own interests by revealing to the board the names and addresses of butchers who do not comply with these regulations. Householders are advised to refer to this list before ordering any cut of beef.
Then follow the prices of some of the most popular cuts in the three first qualities, special, commercial and ordinary.
The hon. member should not be permitted to read his story-book.

I rise to a point of order. My hon. friend is nowhere near the item which is before this committee. The item which we are discussing is pay and allowances for the armed forces. It has nothing to do with rationing or with the subject with which my hon. friend is dealing.
The question which I am discussing now is closely connected with the war effort. We are discussing item No. 3.
No. 2.
Mr. Chairman, with your permission-
I object.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: A point of order has been raised by the minister. I know the committee will realize that it is difficult for a member to confine his remarks to an item of this nature, but I believe I voice the opinion of the committee when I say that while up to the moment we have given considerable latitude in discussion, it is felt that the discussion should now be kept within the limits of the item as much as possible. Otherwise it will be absolutely impossible to make any headway. I think it is the sentiment of the committee that we should get on with the important measure now before the committee.
I do not believe the debate is closed on the point of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I did not say that the debate was closed. I repeat that some latitude must be given, but I believe also that it is the sentiment of every hon. member of the committee that we should get down to earth, if I may use that term, and keep within the limits of the item before the committee.
With your permission I will give the prices.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member was not in the committee previously when we had a general discussion, and it may be the wish of the committee that he be allowed to carry on.
I have the prices of some of the most popular cuts in the three first qualities.
No.
I do not think my hon. friend should be allowed latitude which is denied to the rest of the hon. members. The hon. member knows that his remarks are not relevant to the item before the committee.
I submit respectfully that this is a general discussion.
No.

It is possible to deceive the population for a while, but you cannot do it all the time. The hour is close when the population of this country will exercise its prerogatives against those who have brought these things about. If I am to be prevented from speaking this afternoon, there will be another occasion.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

speechtext: I abide by your decision, Mr. Chairman. At present, we are discussing a resolution calling for the sum of $3,890,000,000 to help the war effort. All [DOT]the clauses of this resolution are interdependent and I do not see why I am not allowed1 to speak just now, since we are to discuss this resolution one clause at a time, as any contract should be examined, because each has some connection with the rest. Has the hon. Minister of National Defence, who is so eager to interrupt me this afternoon, anything to conceal? Referring to the victory of the united nations in Tunisia, he could not spare a word of praise for the brave French soldiers who so gallantly supported the allied advance.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order!
I am speaking on the resolution, Mr. Chairman, and I defy anyone to prove the contrary.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order!

Is there a point of order raised at the moment? By whom, I wonder?
An hon. MEMBER (Translation): By the Chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Laval-Two Mountains is experienced in parliamentary custom, and I would ask him to abide by the procedure I have outlined as Chairman of the committee. We are all in favour of free speech, but I would ask the hon. member to confine himself to the section which is being discussed at present. Otherwise, I shall have to declare the hon. member out of order.

Mr. Chairman, the resolution under discussion just now reads as follows:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide, inter alia,
1.	That sums not exceeding $2,593,333,333.34 (being two-thirds of $3,890,000,000) be granted to His Majesty towards defraying any expenses or making any advances or loans that may be incurred or granted by or under authority of the governor in council during the year ending March 31, 1944, for-
(a)	the security, defence, peace, order and welfare of Canada;
(b)	the .conduct of naval, military and air operations in or beyond Canada;
(c)	promoting the continuance of trade, industry and business communications, whether by means of insurance or indemnity against war risk or in any other manner whatsoever; and
(d)	the carrying out of any measures deemed neeessary or advisable by the governor in council in consequence of the existence of a state of war.
2.	That the governor in council be empowered to raise by way of loan under the provisions of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, 1931, such sum or sums of money, not exceeding in
the whole the sum of $2,593,333,333.34 (being two-thirds of $3,890,000,000) as may be required for the purpose of defraying such expenses or making such advances or loans, the principal and interest of any such loan to be a charge upon and payable . out of the consolidated revenue fund.
3.	That the governor in council be empowered to reexpend, advance or loan moneys that may be received by way of refund or repayment of advances, loans or expenditure under the War Appropriation Acts of 1939 (second session), 1940, 1941, 1942 and 1943.
In accordance with this resolution, Mr. Chairman, I respectfully submit that I have the right to discuss the general aspect of the war policy of the government. At present, we are studying this resolution, irrespective of any particular item. If I have not the right to discuss it, it should be dropped from the order of the day. Why is this resolution on the order of the day if not for discussion?
I was speaking of the omission made by the Minister of National Defence. Was there any reason for it? The most elementary sense of fairness should have impelled the minister to devote to the French heroes a page or at least a few lines of the speech he delivered when narrating the victorious advance of the allies. The victory of the united nations would have been considered just as splendid, and the account of those great military exploits would have been more complete and more authentic. Let us stop distorting facts well-known to all. Let us be honest with ourselves and loyal towards others.
Mr. Chairman, I would ask for silence in the house. Much greater eagerness is shown in having the rules of the house enforced than in keeping order, and I know several hon. members who carry on private conversations at their desks far more often than they speak in the house, not even showing consideration for their colleagues who address them. I will deal with this matter again in the near future.
Let us therefore be honest with ourselves and loyal towards others.
Since it is claimed that the conflict now being waged is a just war whose object is an equitable peace, there should be no injustice toward those who, at the most difficult period of their lives, are nevertheless shedding their blood for the ultimate triumph of the allies and the liberation of their downtrodden country. The omission of the Minister of National Defence is unwarrantable. Can it possibly be a conspiracy of silence about which complaints could rightly be voiced, in the first place, by the French heroes who were its first victims? Three million and a half French-speaking Canadian citizens condemn the minister's omission. No one is more loyally doing his duty in this
War Appropriation-Army

war than the French Canadians. In return, they demand their share of justice or at least of equity. Does anyone 'believe that the government is concerned with that? Not in the least. On the contrary, they tolerate the blackest acts of injustice against citizens of French extraction in Canada. I can give one example out of a great many. Here is what Le Canada, a Montreal newspaper, says in to-day's issue:
Protests against the use of the French language.
Mr. Chairman, you are aware of such a situation, since you are one of the representatives of the minority in Ontario.
In a meeting held in connection with their 67th annual congress, the chapter members of the Western Ontario Royal Black Knights of Ireland have passed a resolution protesting against the use made of the French language in the dominion government offices in Ontario. They have decided to send a copy of that resolution to the Right Hon. Mr. Mackenzie King.
They also protest against the use of French on Canadian Broadcasting Corporation programmes and in the Ontario schools.
This is the kind of treatment we, the pioneers in this country, are receiving. Is there no one in the government to bring to reason these slanderers of three and a half million French Canadians? What is the reaction to these encroachments to national unity, a cause which is so dear to the Prime Minister and the government? The administration does nothing. It persists in following the same policy of non-interference, in spite of the Canada defence regulations and the War Measures Act, which are applied in certain individual cases and to our citizens who are left to languish in internment camps. These regulations are not applied against the supporters of the government. This comedy has lasted long enough. We shall not put up with the gratuitous abuse from these agitators who seem to enjoy the government's protection and we demand justice and reparation. The province of Quebec has been among the first to exceed its objective in the victory loan campaign, but still, the government allows these agitators to abuse its citizens. We protest, and because, this afternoon, I have endeavoured to show to the house that the hon. Minister of National Defence has ignored the heroism of the French element in Tunisia, an effort is made to silence me. Mr. Chairman, I shall not be prevented from expressing my views within the bounds allowed by the rules of the house and I shall stand my ground on this question of paramount importance. I thank you for your forbearance.

This item has to do with pay and allowances for the men in the army. During the discussion yesterday quite a few different points were raised which dealt with the welfare of the men in the forces and their dependents. If the minister will remember, when speaking last week I tried to point out to him and to the committee that thfe national defence department had a responsibility to see to the welfare of the men in the forces, the soldiers and the sailors and the airmen; and I suggested at that time that there were certain grievances which should be righted and certain remedies put into effect: for example, the practice of discharging unfit men too quickly, the question of the changes required in the pension act, the necessity of giving some help to the families of our fighting men in finding homes, the "jokers" in the increase in pay, and questions having to do with dependents' allowance and the protection of the insurance policies which men had taken out before enlistment.
Some of these questions have been dealt with by the minister; most of them have not; and I suggest that the House of Commons should give very careful consideration to the welfare of the men in the forces. They should be helped in cases where their ability to perform a contract has been materially affected by their service. It may be summed up in this way, that these men of ours should be free to devote their entire mental and physical energies to their military tasks. Therefore I suggest that it would be in the best interests of the nation, as well as the just due of these men because of the sacrifice they are making, that they be given legal protection against the economic consequences of their service. This means that where the ability of men in military service and their dependents to meet financial obligations has been materially reduced by service, something should be done by the dominion government.
The government should give them reasonable legal protection against such troubles as evictions, foreclosures, seizures for arrears of taxes, forfeitures of instalment contracts, cancellations of life insurance policies-say, up to a maximum of S10,000-and against judgments or other legal proceedings for debts incurred before they entered military service, and against other embarrassing financial obligations. Such help should, of course, be subject to the express condition that those men who are able to pay shall not evade their obligations because of the help given them, and

War Appropriation-Army
that just protection to creditors should be assured, under the simple and effective procedure which could be furnished by our courts.
It is true that some such protection is given by certain of the provinces.
By all, is it not?
There may be some protection given by all; I am not sure of that.
Not all.
But the protection is only partial; it is not uniform, and in my opinion the dominion should step into the field and give all soldiers, sailors and airmen at least standard protection.
It can be done under the War Measures Act.

Yes. Taking such steps
would certainly be a war measure. The United States has already done that. They have in that country what is known as the Sparkman act, and what I am really advocating to-day is that Canada adopt a Sparkman act suited to our own conditions. This United States act is known officially as the Soldiers' and Sailors' Civil Relief Act of 1940, and it was amended in 1942. The preamble reads as follows:
An Act-
To promote and strengthen the national defence by suspending enforcement of certain civil liabilities of certain persons serving in the military and naval establishments, including the coast guard
I propose to read the first section of the act to hon. members because it gives an idea of the measure I suggest that Canada should have.
May I ask the hon. gentleman a question?
Certainly.
The Sparkman act was before our law clerk and he decided that this parliament had no jurisdiction to pass a similar act.

Well, my suggestion is that such an act can be passed under the War Measures Act. This section reads as follows:
In order to provide for, strengthen and expedite the national defence under the emergent conditions which are threatening the peace and security of the United States-
Mark you, this act was passed in 1940, the year before the United States went to war.
-and to enable the United States the more successfully to fulfil the requirements of the national defence, provision is hereby made to suspend enforcement of civil liabilities, in certain eases, of persons in the military service of
the United States in order to enable such persons to devote their entire energy to the defence needs of the nation, and to this end the following provisions are made for the temporary suspension of legal proceedings and transactions which may prejudice the civil rights of persons in such service during the period herein specified over which this act remains in force.
I do not intend to go over the various provisions, but I should like to point out certain features. One is that the act applies to all of the states, and to proceedings commenced in any court in the United States of America. Another is that Americans serving in the Canadian forces are entitled to the protection of this United States act. Hon. members will find, if they care to look up this act in the library, a lucid explanation of its provisions. In the pamphlet of the United States war department from which I am quoting the purpose of the act is set out.
I quote:
The Soldiers and Sailors Relief Act of 1940 became a part of the laws of the land on October 17, 1940, and will remain in effect until May 15, 1945, or, if the United States is then engaged in war, until such war is terminated by a treaty of peace proclaimed by the President and for six months thereafter. . . . The purpose of the act is to free persons in the military service from harassment and injury to their civil rights during their term of military service and to enable them to devote their entire energy to the war needs of the nation. Generally, the method of the act is to provide for adequate representation of the soldier during his absence, or to authorize the postponement of certain proceedings and transactions until his return from military service.
There is nothing in the act which relieves the soldier from the actual payment of debts or other obligations which he may have incurred before entering the military service. It is only when the soldier's ability to meet his obligations has been impaired, because of military service, that relief is afforded, and this relief is principally against f}ie penalties that would be imposed for non-payment of such obligations. In the traditional American way, questions of the extent to which relief is afforded generally are left to the discretion of our courts of justice.
Our way of looking at things is much the same as the American way and we could very well adopt a measure of this sort. The pamphlet deals with various details of the act. For example, there is a provision that if a soldier makes an agreement after he has enlisted he does not get the protection of the act. There is another which provides that if he is made a defendant in a court action and is unable to appear in court, the court shall appoint an attorney to represent him and protect his interests. Another provision authorizes the court to postpone court proceedings if the soldier who is a party thereto is unable to participate by reason of being in military

War Appropriation-Army

service. For instance, if an American soldier were on service in North Africa I presume he would get the benefit of that provision.

What is the position in
Britain? Have they an equivalent?

I cannot give the hon. member that information; I do not know. Another provision authorizes the court to postpone or vacate execution of any judgment, attachment or garnishee. Another authorizes the court to postpone proceedings for the period of military service, or three months thereafter, or any part thereof. Another excludes the period of military service from computing time under existing or future statutes of limitation, and another provides that interest on the obligations of persons in the military service shall not exceed six per cent per annum, unless the court determines that ability to pay greater interest is not affected by military service. There is a further provision, that a person during his period of military service, or six months thereafter, may apply to a court for relief with respect to his obligations incurred prior to military service, or any tax or assessment whether falling due prior to or during the period of military service. The court may, on certain conditions, stay the enforcement of such obligations.
There are various other provisions, some of which have been made in part by our legislatures. There is provision for stay of eviction where the rental paid for a dwelling is $80 per month or less. The tenant cannot be evicted except by leave of the court which can stay such eviction for three months. There is a provision that contracts for the1 purchase of real and personal property, which originated prior to the period of military service, may not be rescinded, terminated or foreclosed, or the property repossessed, unless by order of the court. Another provision with reference to the soldier or his dependents is that he may terminate a lease by giving a certain length of notice; the idea is to allow the soldier to escape from the onerous terms of a long lease.
There is also a provision with regard1 to insurance, which I think is of great importance and is badly heeded in Canada. It provides for a guarantee by the United States of premium payments on policies up to $10,000, other than United States government life insurance and National Service life insurance, during the period of military service of the insured and two years thereafter. The United States government underwrites the premium. The premiums would be charged against the policy if the policy became pay-

able and what money the government had paid would be deducted. In any event, they would stand as a lien against the policy. The point is, it prevents cancellation of insurance. There are many cases in- Canada, particularly with the older or married men, where they have enlisted and thereby incurred such a reduction in income that they are unable to keep up their insurance policy.

My hon. friend said it
prevents cancellation. He means it prevents cancellation by reason of failure to pay the premium.
Yes.
In many policies there is a difficulty with regard to the policy lapsing owing to war hazard, with the requirement of extra premiums.

As I understand it, this
United States provision would not apply where the policy can be cancelled if a man enlists. I think that is the provision.

Cancellation for want of
premium. Where the payment of premium can save the policy the government guarantees.

Yes. I do not intend to
go into this question at further length. I am merely calling it to the attention of the minister and I suggest -that the taking of such a step now is an essential part of an all-out war effort. The only way our fighting men can get standard protection across Canada is by the dominion government stepping into the field. It can do -that, because it has the power under the provisions of the War Measures Act, and I hope that the government will see fit to bring in some measure like the Sparkman act, without further delay.

Has the act been in force
in the United States long enough, in a given accounting period, to furnish any relative figures as to what the expense of administration- and the extra benefits would represent?

It is not a matter of expense, because the act simply protects the men in the forces. There is not very much government expense involved. It is a matter of the federal government stepping in to protect the rights of its fighting men and to give them a certain backing. The main principle is that where a man's ability to meet his obligations has been impaired by reason of his enlisting in the forces, the government will step in and help him to carry on until after the war. That is the essence of the law. That is the main purpose of it. The same conditions exist in Canada and I think

War Appropriation-Army
we might very well adopt a similar type of legislation here. As I say, it is not a matter of cost because there would not be much cost involved. I imagine a stronger objection would be that it would be interfering with the provinces. The trouble is that the provinces all have different ideas as to the protection they should give the fighting men. Some do not give them very much protection and others quite a bit; further the question has recently become of great importance in the prairie provinces by reason of the disallowance of the Debt Adjustment Act of Alberta; protection for the soldier is contained in these debt adjustments acts in those provinces- at least some protection. It is a question whether or not that has all gone by the boaid. But I do suggest that this is a national question. These troops are the care of the dominion government, not of the provincial governments, and the dominion government should step in and help them.

I hope this matter will be attended to without further delay. I believe the Minister of National Defence has been particularly interested in this question, along with the Minister of Pensions and National Health, and I hope -something may come out of the work of this subcommittee of which they are members. I know in some of the poorer districts of my constituency some of the dependents of the soldiers cannot pay their taxes and the bailiffs have been called in, though the city has been very generous in regard to taxes. The bonus that has been given helps only a small number of people, and is looked upon as charity more than anything else. I believe this parliament could not better occupy itself this session than in considering a national system of insurance, at the same time taking up the other matters mentioned by the hon. member for Vancouver South.

' I should like to associate myself with the remarks of the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church), who I believe has made a definite contribution to the debate this afternoon. I agree entirely that we are not discharging our responsibilities to our soldiers when we leave their property open to the attacks of local tax collectors should arrears develop. In my opinion the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) has performed a real service in bringing this matter to our attention. I should like to ask whether the act he has in mind would merely constitute a stay of proceedings until after the war, or whether it would contain any provision for the central government taking over the responsibility and enabling the soldier to discharge it. During the last war I understand that a good many provinces, or at least some provinces, prevented foreclosures or seizures or sales for taxes, but when the soldier was discharged he had the full responsibility of meeting those accumulated debts, which in many cases constituted an almost intolerable hardship. Does this act provide any safeguard against that sort of thing?

Perhaps the minister can answer that question better than I can, but as I understand it, the Sparkman act does not provide for payment of the indebtedness. It merely provides that a man shall not lose his property, and it also provides that he may not be charged more than six per cent interest during the time he is in the army. For example, if his mortgage calls for interest at the rate of seven per cent he may be charged only six per cent during the time

he is on service. The basic idea is to prevent his losing his property by reason of his service. The minister will correct me if I am wrong, but I believe that is the basis of the act.

I still believe even a provision such as that is altogether inadequate. Our soldiers are not able to accumulate very much money; land when a war stretches out as this one is doing, they become less and less able to draw revenue from any sort of business they might have carried on before going into the army. The men were so poor generally when they went into the army, as a result of the long depression through which we passed, that I think the situation is particularly bad and should be taken care of at once.
I am not entirely in accord with the idea that the dominion should invade the jurisdiction of the provinces in this respect; I think the dominion has exercised discretion in this regard. I believe, however, that an enabling act might be passed under which the dominion would cooperate with the provinces. I doubt very much if there is a provincial government in Canada at the present time that would not readily cooperate with the dominion government in any reasonable, feasible scheme for the protection of the soldiers.

May I add only a word to what has been said by other hon. members. I think everyone in the house is in favour of the protection of the property of the men in the armed forces. But, as some other hon. members have said, it is a question of civil rights, and civil rights are within the control of the provinces. I believe therefore that our best plan would be that of applying our energy toward influencing the governments in the different provinces, rather than discussing the question here, when we have no power in the matter.
I note that only yesterday the government of Quebec brought down a similar measure. I do not have the details of it, but I understand the measure provides that no mortgage can be foreclosed against a farm belonging to a man in the armed forces, including all the services. In respect of a lawsuit involving property, permission to sue must be obtained from the superior court before action can be started. That is a step in the right direction.

That is in respect of a mortgage, or a charge against land; or does it apply to a simple contract?

War Appropriation-Army
I have not the bill before me, but I believe it applies to any lawsuit involving property. Concerning mortgages on property, that is definitely so.
There is the same provision in Ontario, I think.

Then, with respect to other lawsuits, permission has to be obtained) from a judge before a lawsuit involving property belonging to a man in the armed forces can be initiated. So that I think we are all in _ agreement, on whatever side of the house we may be, that it is a question of who has power to do it. In the federal parliament I do not believe we are empowered to invade provincial rights in respect of questions of this kind.

Does the hon. member not think that the dominion would have power to pass under the War Measures Act a law such as I have suggested? The United States federal government had much the same difficulty to overcome. Three years ago, however, they passed the Sparkman act, and their situation has greatly improved.

I am sure that under the War Measures Act the government has power over the life and death of everyone in the country. But I do think it should use such power sparingly. When it comes to the consideration of a question so serious as that of property and civil rights of citizens, we would gain much by obtaining the good-will of all the provinces. Suggestions could be sent and meetings held among the governments, to arrive at an understanding, rather than force it through under the War Measures Act.

In 1940 most of the veterans' organizations in Canada were sending resolutions to the provincial governments and to members of parliament-I know I received many of them-asking that a moratorium be granted in respect to members of the services who had purchased homes and obligated themselves to make certain monthly payments which were not possible under army pay. The matter was referred to Ottawa and I took it up with the Department of Finance. The minister advised me it was a matter of provincial jurisdiction. The matter has dragged along, and evidently nothing has been done about it. I do not know anything about the Sparkman act in the United States, but I do know that the government of New Zealand has provided a supplementary grant up to $15 a week to all members of the forces, which is available to take care of cases of this kind. Could some such machinery not be provided by the federal government in Canada?
I have in mind a case I took up with the Department of National Defence about two months ago. A man overseas was notified that his property was in jeopardy because of outstanding taxes. Through the representations I made a supplementary grant was allowed and the soldier's property protected.
I was so advised by the department. Of course the grant was limited.
Was that by this government?

Yes. May I support what was said by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green). This is a matter of deep concern to the members of the forces, and one which has caused considerable agitation in veterans' organizations. If a little country like New Zealand can pass legislation granting that amount of money to take care of contingencies of this kind, I cannot see why the Canadian government could not take similar action. My experience leads me to believe that there may be some provision which can be reached in a roundabout way, but it is hard to get it. The process is slow. Any man who is overseas, prepared to lay down his life for freedom and democracy, should not be placed in the position of learning that the home he has left behind him has been threatened because of unpaid taxes.
Provincial governments are not going to do anything about it. Anyone who offers that argument is merely passing the buck. It is not a matter to-day of recognizing the rights of provinces respecting private property. What we are arguing for is the protection of the property of the man who has gone overseas to fight for the institutions of our country. There is no valid argument for the provinces stepping into the picture, because the national government has invaded practically every field of revenue the provinces had. I believe we should make some definite arrangement with respect to protecting the property of men who have gone overseas.

In my submission the argument adduced by the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Picard) is scarcely in line with the conditions which the government and the country face. As was so well said by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), this government has invaded the fields of greatest consequence, and perhaps in the remaining provincial fields there is not the same opportunity of taking action in respect to the matter raised by the hon. member for Vancouver South. I am not at all impressed by the suggestion that we should stand on technicalities when we are dealing with matters affecting the men and women who are fighting for us. It seems to me that
IFar Appropriation-Army

to raise the question of property and civil rights and jurisdiction given under the British North America Act to the various governments in Canada is straining the point much too far.
* Perhaps the best argument against leaving this matter to the provinces is the fact that in several of the provinces they are only now initiating legislation. What is going to happen to the man overseas who loses his home prior to the time of the legislation becoming effective? It is all very well to say that the legislation could be made retroactive. But even with a retroactive provision, it is very difficult to return matters to their original condition. For that reason I say the government must accept a considerable share of responsibility for, first of all, not having exercised its power and jurisdiction under the War Measures Act to do what has been suggested. I think no one would quarrel with the government's power, and this action should have been taken at the beginning of the war. That was the time to do it, because it was tied up with our whole war plan. It is a case of too little and too late. It seems to me at this particular time the government must assess to themselves very broad responsibilities with respect to this particular matter.
I agree with what one of the previous speakers said, that the provinces may legislate; but have we any guarantee that there will be any uniformity in the provincial legislation? Have we any guarantee as to the extent or degree of enthusiasm which will be put into the enforcement of the act by the different provinces?
There is no enforcement?

Perhaps the minister does not understand my point but I shall come to it in a moment. These men are from Canada, not simply from one of the provinces. Keeping that squarely in mind, is there any reason why a man who has volunteered his services and finds some court order against him when in England should suffer by virtue of the fact that he comes from one province rather than from another? It seems to me that the thread of the assumption of responsibility runs through the whole matter. I do not think the dominion government can toss this aside on the basis of its being a matter of property and civil rights which come under the jurisdiction of the provinces. Whoever it was in the cabinet who suggested that this was a provincial matter, I do not know, but this responsibility ought to be brought out in the open. Had this same point been raised in connection with many matters relating to our war effort we would have had a much poorer effort by virtue of it.

This is a national issue, therefore two things should be done or should have been done long before this. Either there should be uniformity of legislation by the provinces across Canada, or there should be legislation enacted, or at least orders in council issued under the provisions of the War Measures Act. Someone has said that we might be touching property, but where the question of property and the question of human values come into conflict, surely we have gone sufficiently far along the road, particularly in this war-time emergency, to place some measure of emphasis upon human values rather than upon property values. It seems to me that that is the root of the proposal which has been advanced so well by the hon. member for Vancouver South.
It is our duty to see that our soldiers are well protected in the way of reinforcements and the necessary equipment and the best generalship we can provide, but at the same time we should give the necessary protection so far as their home affairs are concerned. In most cases these men are civilian soldiers. When the war is over they expect to come back to take their places in civilian life. Not only is protection comparable to that afforded by the Sparkman act necessary; we should be prepared not only to preserve the property of the soldier but also to see that his morale is kept up. The minister should give careful consideration to doing what must be done to provide protection comparable to or even greater than that given by other nations. This is not only the responsibility of the government; it is their duty, and I ask them to accept it.

I concur in what has been said already on the subject now under discussion, and particularly with what the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Black-more) has said to the effect that it is not sufficient just to stay proceedings against a soldier while he is overseas. A fact that we should keep in mind is that many of these men undertook commitments before enlisting which they were justified in undertaking, commitments which they were able to meet out of their civilian earnings but which they cannot meet out of their soldiers' pay. It behooves us as a government to adopt some measures to safeguard these men against losses which they may incur because of these commitments.
Reference has been made to New Zealand. My information is that in that country the commitments which a soldier undertook before enlisting and which he can show he was able to take care of at that time are assumed by his government while he is in the army. I

War Appropriation-Army
understand that recent provisions have been made in Great Britain for something much along the same line. Surely, as some hon. members have suggested this afternoon, we are not going to let the provisions of the British North America Act, in so far as they concern property, interfere with our duty and moral Obligation to the men who are protecting this very property and but for whose services this property would be worth little today, to the province, to the individual or to anyone else.

I desire to associate myself with the recommendations made by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green), and particularly those made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis). The hon. member for Cape Breton South suggested to the minister that he should endeavour to embody in legislation or in an order in council under federal jurisdiction the type of relief we have been discussing. I believe in peace time we should be zealous about not encroaching upon the purely provincial jurisdiction which is granted by the British North America Act, but if I may be bold enough to offer a suggestion to the minister and to the Minister of Justice, and to the advisers whom they may consult, the question of jurisdiction might be covered in this way. If there be conflict under the British North America Act between a particular measure introduced by us and one introduced by a province, we have been told more than once by the privy council that the very pith and substance and the real purpose of the legislation must first be looked to, and then if there be conflict in the carrying out of the real purpose and the federal act or order in council should appear incidentally to infringe upon subjects purely provincial, the larger federal jurisdiction must prevail. If I am right in that view of the law, then applying that test to this legislation it is primarily, it is essentially so far as its purpose is concerned, purely a war measure. If there were no war there would be no army tc protect, there would be no need for the legislation at all. But it is beyond question a war measure. I deplore the tendency-the minister is in no way responsible for it-to tell us, as we have been told once or twice in this house, that we must not do this or that 'because it is a provincial matter. I have in mind particularly the effort that was made by some members of this house to persuade the administration to raise the old age pension from twenty to thirty dollars a month and to lower the age limit. This is not the time to discuss that problem; I refer to it merely incidentally, although I propose to see that
the problem is further discussed in this house. But I am bitterly opposed to being told that it is purely a provincial matter, and therefore, as a member said, we pass the buck and refuse to carry out our responsibilities in that regard.
I do not think there will be any constitutional difficulty. It is particularly a war measure for this further reason. We are inviting the young men, the married1 men, the ablebodied men of this country to join up voluntarily in order that our reinforcements may be provided beyond peradventure, and when we invite them so to do will anyone suggest that we are not able to assure them that if they are in financial difficulties the money lenders and the usurers shall not take advantage of them when they are away on the country's business?
Or the tax collector.

Or the tax collector, or any of those who want to enforce obligations regardless of whether or why the man is unable to pay. Therefore, again, it is esentially a war measure in that respect, and I want to support such proper relief as the minister with his advisers can devise in order to carry out in spirit the proposals put forward by the member for Vancouver South.

Mr. Chairman, I feel like complimenting the member for Vancouver South upon introducing this subject, and I hope some good will result from it. Had it not been f(jr the government's decision at the beginning of the session not to permit the debating of private members' resolutions, the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) would have had this matter discussed earlier in the session. During the great war he was known throughout Canada as the soldier's friend, a title he richly deserved, one that he won for himself by his great efforts on behalf of the soldiers. In his resolution he calls for all that has been urged this afternoon-insurance for the soldiers, protection from foreclosure, more adequate and improved housing for the soldiers and their families. During his administration as mayor of Toronto he carried through city council a measure granting to the family of each soldier killed overseas one thousand dollars, and I remember what a benefit that insurance of one thousand dollars was, particularly in the riding which I represent, from which so many soldiers went overseas, many of whom were killed, and the benefit it was to soldiers' families throughout the city generally. The hon. member for Broadview, had he been given the privilege of debating his resolution, would have strongly
War Appropriation-Army

argued, as he did to-day, and as did the hon. member for Vancouver South and other members, that soldiers should be insured and that their families and dependents should be adequately provided for and protected from eviction and have more adequate and improved housing, and that his proposals should prevail not only during the war but for six months thereafter. I rise to associate myself with those who have preceded me in supporting the suggestion of the hon. member for Vancouver South that the government should bring in a sytem of insurance for the soldiers.

May I say
just a word in support of the arguments which have been placed before the minister with reference to giving protection and assistance to men in the armed services who may own a home or a farm. It seems to me that there are two questions involved.
First is the question of protection. That is a very important matter to the men who have joined the armed services from the prairies. Many of these young men were just starting up on a farm. They might have been buying the farm. They might have been buying machinery on time. There might be a mortgage on the farm. They might have borrowed money to build a house. Now the farm is rented out or being run by relatives. In some cases the soldier just walked off and left the farm, to join up. The very least they have a right to expect is that they will enjoy all the possible protection which this parliament can give them while they are rendering the best possible service that any man can give to his day and generation.
It seems to me that the constitutional objection is not a serious one. We used to believe that under the section of the British North America Act dealing with property and civil rights the entire matter of protection of these rights rested with the provincial legislatures, but we have found within the last year that that was not a sound contention, because the debt adjustment legislation of Alberta, and incidentally of Saskatchewan and Alberta, was found to be ultra vires, and in the interim while other legislation was being prepared the Minister of Justice himself had an order in council passed temporarily granting a stay of proceedings in order to keep the farmers on the farm as efficient producers. So that increasingly a large part of the responsibility for giving protection to people on their farms and in their homes has already been assumed by the federal government. Now, if the federal government can take steps, as it has already done, to give protection to a farmer to keep

him on the land as an efficient producer, certainly it can use the same power to give protection to the soldier overseas and see to it that when he comes back his home or his farm will still belong to him and will not have been taken by a creditor, a mortgagee or tax collector.
There is a second aspect of this question which ought not to be lost sight of, it was mentioned by the member for Cape Breton South. This parliament has the responsibility to do more than merely give the soldier protection. It ought to do something to help reduce the soldier's obligations, particularly accumulated-taxes that may have piled up on his property. That has been done in New Zealand, which pays up to a maximum of $15 a week to help meet the commitments accruing from time to time on the property of soldiers overseas. It will be difficult enough for a man coming back from overseas to become reestablished in civilian life, without being faced with an accumulation of debt which has piled up against his home or his property. It will be well if the ministers will make some investigation into the provisions of the measure passed by the government of New Zealand by which they undertake some responsibility for reducing this burden of debt against soldiers' property, in order that when the men come back they can once more take up their role in civilian life without a burden of debt.

We have been talking about protection and assistance for men in the armed forces, and there seems to be a tendency to try to make people believe that it is only on one side of the house that this feeling is held. We should make it very plain that we all are in favour of a measure of this land being passed to protect the men in the armed forces; it is just a question of procedure, as to how it should be done.
I was surprised to hear the leader of the opposition treat the British North America Act in such a light fashion. He and his predecessors have often rested their arguments on the sanctity of the British North America Act and many of its clauses. The leader says that somebody in the cabinet should be responsible, but I do not think any member of the cabinet is old enough to be responsible for what is in the British North America Act. They cannot but follow the constitution; otherwise we would have one constitution for a time of peace and one for a time of war-which is already in the process of erection.
May I ask the hon. member a question?

Yes.

War Appropriation-Army
Is he arguing now against the constitutionality of the War Measures Act?

Not at all. But I say this
should be applied sparingly, when strictly needed; and when it comes to a matter of property rights we could arrive at exactly the same thing in another way. I favour the suggestions for protection and assistance which have been made this afternoon. Up to now five provinces have passed such legislation. I believe that, of those five measures, three at any rate have been made retroactive, so that only four of the provinces have to be approached in order that the question may be dealt with through the proper procedure according to the British North America Act.

Will my hon. friend
permit a question? Would he deem it to be contrary to the British North America Act if the dominion government made a grant to the provinces with which they would be able to advance $15 a week to the soldiers who enlisted within their boundaries, as New Zealand has done?

That would be along the
same line as the Old Age Pension Act. There is nothing to prevent us from passing such an act, but we cannot force the provinces to apply it or to enact similar legislation. We had unfortunately in Quebec this situation, that although it was entitled to the benefits of the Old Age Pension Act, the then supposedly Liberal premier of the government obstinately refused to apply it. As to our right to pass such a measure, as suggested by the leader of the Social Credit party, there is no doubt in my mind that we have the right to pass it.

May I ask one more
question? Does the hon. member believe there is any province in Canada which would not accept $15 a week for each of the soldiers enlisted from its territory, and agree to give it to him on condition that he needed it to discharge his obligations?

I am not in a position to
say what is in the minds of all the provinces. I suppose that in all the provinces people would be satisfied to give that $15 to soldiers, just as everybody would have liked to get that $25 bonus which was promised in a certain province but which nobody ever got. So that the same thing might happen with regard to a $15 bonus.
But to revert to the question with which I am dealing, somebody has stated that there is a duty and a moral obligation towards the soldiers, and I think it is so. But the duty and the moral obligation do not warrant a government setting aside the constitution when
other remedies can be found and can be easily applied. The provincial governments have only to be approached, probably, to pass such measures and enact them immediately, thus obtaining the same result as we would obtain by invading their property rights under the War Measures Act, which I think would be an unfortunate thing. We should arrive at the aim which we all-not only those on one side of the house-desire to reach, namely to protect and assist the soldiers. We all share the same views. It is entirely a question of procedure, of how to do the thing properly.

I should like to associate myself with those who are placing these representations before the government with regard to greater protection for our soldiers serving overseas. I think it is a national, not a provincial responsibility. It is true that so far as the British North America act is concerned it might be treated as a provincial responsibility. I am not greatly concerned about that,	nor would I	dare to approach itfrom the	legal	point	of view.	But asapparently	it has	been	recognized	in fiveof the provinces that there is a responsibility on	either	the	provincial	or the
federal authority to take care of and give proper protection to our soldiers, that having been settled, the dominion government could very well find a way, as they did in 1919 in dealing with old age pensions, to assume a responsibility which I feel is theirs. It is unfair to place the responsibility on the provinces, taking into consideration the enlistments of the various provinces and their ability to meet the financial obligations entailed. I have in mind my own province, that of Nova Scotia, where there were enlistments of something like 44.5 per cent, compared with some other provinces which had a very much smaller percentage of enlistments. It would be unfair to Nova Scotia to require them to assume a responsibility which, as I said before, appears to me to be a national responsibility.
I compliment the hon. member for Vancouver South for bringing this matter before the committee. It is a constructive thought and one which I think the Minister of National Defence and the cabinet as a whole should go into very carefully, with a view to bringing, if at all possible, about the results desired. I am not an authority on either the British North America Act or the War Measures Act, but I sincerely hope the minister will give the matter careful consideration with a view to providing the protection to which, I think, the soldiers serving overseas are entitled.
