It is well that the government should have the views of various sections of the house regarding fair and just treatment of our soldiers in this war. Notwithstanding what the hon. member for Beilechasse has said, in dealing with soldiers' problems, necessity should know no law in giving them fair play. I have here a copy of the opinion of our legal department as to the powers and functions of this parliament to pass such a measure as the so-called Sparkman act, which was referred to by the hon. member for Vancouver South. Last fall I sent the joint law clerks of the House of Commons a copy of this United States act, and on January 13, 1943, they wrote me the following letter:
We have given consideration to your letter of the 11th instant, in regard to the introduction of legislation in parliament similar to the U.S. Soldiers' and Sailors' Civil Relief Act of 1940. Whether such legislation is within the jurisdiction of parliament is not competent for us to decide and our opinion would carry no weight. If we were asked for an unofficial opinion, we would be inclined to say that such legislation is within the competence of parliament. The government under the authority of the War Measures Act has legislated by order in council in respect to the control of rents along similar lines to that contained in the U.S. act.
The United States act covers a very wide field indeed, and similar legislation, if passed by parliament, would no doubt encroach upon and to a great extent wipe out the peace-time jurisdiction and jurisprudence of the provinces.
We doubt that the government would consider such a revolutionary step without first consulting with the provinces. We would not undertake the responsibility of drafting a bill of this kind without first consulting the provincial governments as to its effect upon the many persons and interests and municipalities involved. Its effect upon the rules, practice and procedure in the courts would also be a serious matter. We, of course, are not in a position to take up these matters with the provincial governments.
We return herewith your copy of the Soldiers' and Sailors' Civil Relief Act of 1940.
I believe the people will support the government if they pass a national statute to cover this matter, as they did for a national system of unemployment insurance. I am sure they would get the support of the provinces, so that long deferred justice would be given the soldiers and their dependents.

This matter should be
approached from the national rather than the provincial point of view, because we have to establish a set of uniform rules if we are to put into effect the suggestions made by the various speakers in favour of this particular type of legislation. At the present time, as indicated by one speaker, there are certain acts which were passed by a number of the

provinces-I believe, by four provinces-but these acts are not uniform, and, in some instances they do not give that protection to the soldier which I think they should.
There is this point that seems to be of the utmost importance. If we have a soldier coming from one part of the country who enjoys one form of protection and another soldier from another part of the country receiving a different form of protection we are bound to have discontent should that state of affairs continue. I understand that in British Columbia there is an act that protects the soldiers with respect to real property, whereas in another province they have an act that protects the soldier not only with respect to real property but with respect to chattels, there being conditional sale agreements, lien agreements and so on. They prevent the seizure of chattels for arrears of rent.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: It is taxes and mortgages in British Columbia.

In British Columbia they do not grant any remission of taxes, whereas in Saskatchewan it is provided that there shall be remission of taxes up to $125 a year. A soldier coming from British Columbia and discussing the matter with a friend from Saskatchewan will be quite discontented and will feel that he has been rather badly dealt with, because in his case all they do is to forestall the day for the collection of taxes, whereas in the other province they write them off to a certain extent. There are two very important reasons why this matter should be passed by this parliament now. The protection is required now, not later, and if we wait until we get agreement on the part of the various provinces it will take a considerable time. They will have to get together to discuss the matter and draft legislation, and if the past can be taken as a precedent it will require many months to reach agreement. The legislatures will not be meeting again until next January or February, and the matter will be delayed for that length of time. I suggest that for these reasons it is of the utmost importance that we do something about approaching this matter from the national point of view.

The only reason why I rise on this occasion is the fact that there have been three cases in my riding where two farms and one home were to be taken over but for the intervention of certain friends of the soldiers. In one instance the soldier before going overseas had almost

War Appropriation-Army
paid for his home, but owing to sickness in the family it was necessary to put on an extra mortgage, and when he went overseas he had also to give up his insurance policy to help to pay his debts. Here was a hard-working man who, on account of sickness and hard luck in the family, was unable to get ahead) and pay his debts. Fortunately friends came to the rescue and took this mortgage, and they have it at the present time and are keeping it without charging the soldier's wife any interest. The agreement is that they will hold it until the war is over and the soldier is able to pay. On two farms about which I know quite a bit practically the same thing happened. These were good farmers. They had put on mortgages, however, owing to the fact that there was sickness and debt in the family. In one case it was a veteran who had to mortgage his place and friends came across. They are holding these two farms at the present time for these soldiers. These men are all overseas and had been extremely worried about conditions at home, so much so that their wives felt that they could not really do a good job. These soldiers were worried about their families, and wrote not only to myself but to many people in our district asking what could be done. You cannot have satisfied soldiers overseas if they are worrying about conditions at home, and that is one reason why I support the hon. member for Vancouver South.
In connection with the income tax I referred to the question of insurance policies, and I mentioned one man who had a $7,000 policy. He now gets $1.30 a day. He was unable to carry that policy because, although he left a job paying $4,000 a year, he now gets SI.30 or $1.40 a day. I wish to support the hon. member in what he has put forward. In my opinion the matter is a federal one, because these men and women in the armed forces- and the women should be included'-are paid by the federal government and not by the provinces. They are employees of this government and we should look after them.

In view of the representations made in this matter, I hope that the minister will indicate his attitude toward the suggestions that have been brought forward. There is one particular kind of life insurance to which I would refer, on account of cases which have been brought to my attention. I put certain questions on the order paper in this regard, but the return has not yet been brought down, although the Secretary of State informs me that it is being proceeded with. I refer to group insurance policies of the kind
that are held jointly by employees who work for a company. I am told that in a case of this kind when a man takes leave of absence and enlists, his policy is discontinued. My information is that it is discontinued whether or not he is able financially to carry his portion of the insurance. There must be a good deal of this sort of insurance, and I hope that such insurance will be included in any investigation the government may make in an effort to carry out the representations that have been submitted to them. There are one or two other matters relating to dependents' allowances on which I wish to say a word or two, but perhaps it is just as well not to interrupt this discussion now.
Mr. RALSTON1: First, I wish to say that the matter has been very much to the fore for a good while, particularly in connection with the administration of the three service departments. I have had conferences with the other ministers of the service departments and also with.the Minister of Finance, and on January 15 I think I addressed all attorneys-general or provincial premiers with regard to existing or prospective legislation the enactment of which they might be considering.
Was that January 15 last?

Yes. The situation is not that the dominion government or the dominion parliament has not jurisdiction, or that there is anyone in the cabinet who would1 suggest that federal action may not be taken. What we are doing is entering a field which is distinctly provincial under the British North America Act, and it would seem that the least we could do would be to consult the provinces and find out what action they have in mind.
The government did not do that in connection with the wartime prices and trade board order concerning rents.

Creditors are distinctly within the sphere of provincial legislation. Simply to step in and say that all creditors' claims shall be barred, particularly when some provinces have had moratorium legislation on their statute books since 1939, would seem to be undesirable. Therefore we endeavoured to ascertain what degree of uniformity could be attained by the provinces, in order that the dominion might better decide what action we ourselves could or should take.

Did the order in council passed by the Minister of Justice not do just that, stop creditors from collecting debts from farmers in the western provinces?
War Appropriation-Army

That is correct, but I am saying that in this case we had provincial legislation of this very kind in this very field, and it did seem desirable to ascertain how far the provinces were prepared to go with respect to creditors in each province, before we finally decided what the dominion could do. I do not think there can be any criticism of that policy. It has not delayed anything, but it does seem to me the proper way to proceed, particularly where legislation already exists in some provinces. I think I am in a position to say that to-day every province has moratorium legislation which is available to service men.
Has New Brunswick?
Yes. I think the bill in Quebec has just passed the legislative assembly and is now before the legislative council.
Do any of these provincial acts go as far-as the Sparkman act?

No. There are some special features in the Sparkman act, particularly that to which my hon. friend referred, the matter of keeping insurance alive, which are not in any of the provincial acts. I think none of the acts go farther than to enact moratorium legislation. The features of difference are generally how the moratorium is effected'; that is to say, whether a man is prevented from bringing action at all or whether there shall be a stay of proceedings after the action is commenced, and the other feature in which there is difference is the sort of debts to which the moratorium applies. Some apply only to real property; I think one applies only to home property. Many apply to taxes. Some apply to simple contract debts, and some do not.
Did I understand the minister to say that the first time the dominion government had conferred with the provinces in an official way in connection with this matter was on January 15 of this year?

I cannot say what the dominion government did before; I am telling the committee that I took this personal action on January 15, after the matter had been discussed by the government in the light of the fact that legislation had been passed in some of the provinces and that other provinces were considering such legislation. I addressed those letters on January 15. I am not going to say that was the first time it was considered, by any means.
Does the minister know of any previous conferences that were held?

I cannot recall any now. As a matter of fact, the Minister of Finance had been dealing with the matter up to that time; after all, it was a matter of finance and affecting credit.
Just for the record, so that hon. members may realize what these differences are, I should like to place them on Hansard. With regard to method, the provinces of Saskatchewan, Alberta, Prince Edward Island, Manitoba and British Columbia prohibit the taking of action without permission. In Ontario, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia the action is allowed to proceed, but the 'judge is given jurisdiction to order a stay of proceedings. With regard to scope, all the provinces give protection in actions or proceedings relating to mortgages and agreements of sale. Some provinces, like Ontario, deal only with such actions. Prince Edward Island, Manitoba and Alberta include all actions and proceedings with respect to any debt or obligation. This is a feature in which I am sure the committee is very much interested, whether or not any moratorium legislation shall apply simply to home property, to real property and leases, or to all debts and obligations. In some provinces no protection is given against obligations incurred after enlistment. As I caught it from my hon. friend, I do not think the Sparkman act applies to obligations incurred after enlistment.
I think that is right.

Ontario gives no protection in the case of mortgages entered into after March 10, 1943, which I think is the date the legislation was passed; and a stay can be granted only if default is attributable to the fact that an applicant is a member of the forces. That is so under the Sparkman act also, if I remember it correctly. The ground of relief is that the embarrassment has been due to war circumstances or conditions. By the way, that is the situation in the United Kingdom, to which reference was made by one hon. member during the course of the debate. The United Kingdom act does not apply only to members of the forces, though they come within the general class. "Any person who is in serious financial difficulties owing to war circumstances"; that is the general formula for relief. That is the Liabilities Wartime Adjustment Act, 1941, chapter 24 of the statutes of the United Kingdom.
I suppose that would cover people who were bombed out.

I suppose it would; of course they had the war risk insurance in addition to that. In Saskatchewan it seems

War' Appropriation-Army
to be immaterial when the obligation was incurred. Some of the statutes extend protection to dependents and personal representatives, while others do not. With one exception the provinces extend protection to members of the forces of his majesty's allies, but no province gives protection to other than a member of the forces, his estate or his dependents.
All these statutes have been the subject of examination by a -responsible committee which is headed by the deputy minister of justice and on which are representatives of the armed services, the Department of Pensions and National- Health, the Department of Finance and the superintendent of insurance. That committee has now reported. The report has not as yet been considered by the government, but it will be considered very shortly. I can assure the committee that all the matters which have been referred to this afternoon will be given active study in -connection with the report of the committee. I anticipate that action will be taken along lines which I feel ought to meet the situation.
Just in closing I wish to say that members of the committee will realize that in connection with legislation of this kind we are calling u-pon the creditor to do a good deal. It is the creditors, not the public generally, who are being asked to make the sacrifice or the adjustment; it is the individual creditor. In other words, he may be regarded as in bad luck because he happened to be the creditor of a man who afterward- became a -member of the forces, and upon whose obligations a legal bar is placed. I mention this because it seems to me that is the feature which-and I speak personally-does make it desirable that the federal authorities take some responsibility in the matter. It ought not simply to be regarded as a contribution by creditors, and nothing else. In that connection responsibility would be asserted by endeavouring to make whatever relief there is uniform across the country, and not have it dependent solely upon the judgment-if I may put it in that way-or the views of the various provincial legislatures. There may be different situations in different provinces which, while requiring a proper consideration from a provincial point of view, would not have quite the same significance when one considers the problem in the light of its relationship to those who, for the time being, are directly responsible to the federal government. I can only assure the committee that every study will be made of the matter, and active consideration will be given to it.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: May I be permitted to answer an interruption of the hon. member for Wey-burn, when he suggested that the Minister of Justice had- recommended an order in council empowering the -courts in the three western provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, to stay proceedings for the foreclosure of mortgages against farms, or the cancellation of agreements for the sale of farm properties. I hope the hon. member did not wish to imply that there was any inconsistency between that course -and the course being discussed by the Minister of National Defence, in saying that the provinces were being consulted. I am sure the hon. member well knows that that order in council was recommended at the express request of the governments of the three provinces concerned.

I was not suggesting that there was any inconsistency. I was pointing out that since the Minister of Justice had power to recommend that order in council, he certainly had power to recommend a similar order in council covering the men in the armed services.
The Minister of National Defence referred to the provincial acts. I am wondering if any steps have been taken to ascertain their validity. If I remember correctly, in the decisions handed down with respect to the debt adjustment legislation of Alberta one of the reasons given for declaring that legislation ultra vires was that it denied to creditors access to the courts, where they might secure redress. I do not think anyone has taken this legislation to the courts. But if that were done, the same ground might be used to declare this legislation ultra vires, and these men would not have the protection mentioned by the minister.

One or two of the acts have existed for some time. Apparently there has been no attack, or at least if there has been it has been unsuccessful. The British Columbia act was passed in 1934, and the Alberta act in 1940. So far as I know, no attack has been made upon them. The Manitoba act is chapter 11 of their statutes for 1940. The Saskatchewan act is found at chapter 73 of their 1942 statutes, and the remaining acts are in the current year.

The debt
adjustment acts were older than that, and still they were declared ultra vires.

I can only say I know of no attack having been made upon these acts.
War Appropriation-Army
The minister said nothing about the protection of insurance policies.

The committee's report is *being considered in the light of all that has been said. There will be a study of the Sparkman act, a study of the United Kingdom act and of the New Zealand act. Recommendations are now being considered.

We have had from the minister an interesting statement of the action which he instituted on January 15. Did that action arise out of anything within the department, or did it arise from the fact that on December 15 this party declared for this very kind of action. It is just another case of the government's stepping in when prompted by political opponents to bring in a great reform.
The question of jurisdiction has not bothered hon. members opposite, notwithstanding the plea of the hon. member for Bellechasse. I am surprised that the minister has gone to such pains in consulting the provinces. I recall that for the relief of civilians in the matter of rents this government, under the authority of the War Measures Act, stepped into the provincial arena, and invaded the rights of creditors, without consulting the provinces. So that I am just wondering if it is on account of the fear of invasion of the principle of autonomy, so loudly claimed by one or two of the provinces, that the minister has had these consultations.
As a matter of fact, I have yet to learn that any of the provincial legislation-at least I believe this to be so in respect of the maritime provinces-has been effective. Certainly I do not think it covers the field. The minister himself has indicated that there is grave doubt in the minds of most members of the government as to whether the field is covered, because the whole thing has been referred for study to the departmental committee headed by the deputy minister of justice, and it is quite apparent there is no uniformity. Furthermore, as the minister has said, not one of the provinces is assuming any financial responsibility for the benefit of these returned men. On the theory that there is a financial responsibility, and this being, in the wmrds of the hon. member for Parry Sound, a war measure and for war relief, I say this ought to be done by the dominion, irrespective of the provinces. Let us have uniformity of legislation.
The party to which I belong declared long ago for a comprehensive piece of legislation which would cover returned men, on the theory that the returned man is making a

great sacrifice, and that the dominion government, which has invaded every field of provincial jurisdiction, should assume responsibility, irrespective of the rights of the provinces. We beg the minister to bring down at the earliest possible date a comprehensive scheme which will not only cover the rights in respect of property, which is only one of the factors, but protect the soldier with respect to all other obligations. When I refer to property I mean real property. Such provision should protect the soldier with regard to all other obligations he may have, w.ith the assurance that when he does come back he will not have this huge load of debt about which the hon. member for Lethbridge spoke this afternoon.
The people of Canada will stand behind parliament in bringing down a measure of alleviation for those of our soldiers who find themselves in difficult positions. But I do not wish anyone to have the idea that this sort of thing ought to be automatic. There ought to be cause shown in each case, as is done under the Sparkman act. That measure is not automatic. It operates on cause shown, and if it is demonstrated that a man's position will be jeopardized, in such an event the aid provided is given.
The nation will be behind the government which tackles this matter man-fashion. The nation will be behind the minister-although I think it is now rather late-if he does something about it. I cannot imagine anything *which could be more discouraging to the soldier overseas than to receive some day a letter from his wife stating that the bailiff had called, or that the municipal tax collector was threatening to sell his property. Nothing could be more distressing, with the exception of the news that some other man had run away with his wife. That of course, would be worse-and it has happened.

Depending
upon the wife.
Mr. HANSON ' (York-Sunbury): Yes, depending upon the wife. But it would be disheartening to the soldier to learn that his wife had been unfaithful while he was overseas. I have had some very heart-x-ending cases brought to my attention, but that is by the way. I am not qualified to speak for everybody, but from the expressions of opinion we have heard this afternoon I think I can say that hon. members on all sides of the house will be behind the administration if they seize this opportunity to fulfil a national responsibility. That is what it is. Having heard his resume of what the provinces have

War Appropriation-Army
done, I say to the minister candidly that it falls far short of what is necessary. We shall have to do something better if we want to look these men in the face when they come back.

I do not want to rob my hon. friend or the party with which he is connected of any credit which he feels should come to them, but I did not .think that this matter was being discussed in a party spirit.
It was in our platform.

I assure my hon. friend that I missed it. I was looking back through the correspondence, and just on this file I found some memoranda as early as September, long before the Winnipeg convention was held. At that time the deputy minister of justice had prepared a memorandum at the request of the Minister of Finance with regard to moratorium legislation. Even though it may rob my hon. friend's party of some glory for having initiated this idea, I must say to him that the action taken was not due to the Winnipeg convention.
This matter has received the careful, thorough and, if I may so so, intelligent consideration by the committee which its importance demanded. We realized the degree of federal responsibility in connection with it; we realized the situation which had to be met. I may remind the committee that measures for assistance of members of the forces in financial difficulties and their dependents came earlier than January of this year. The dependents' board of trustees was set up nearly a year and a half ago. That board has taken care of many types of cases which are not taken care of by the legislation of any other country. In 'cases of hardship they make special grants, just as my hon. friend suggests should be done. When a case is proved, it is attended to promptly. I want the committee to realize that this special form of relief which has proved most effective does not exist in other countries.
In many cases the dependents' board of trustees may be able to deal with the situation, but that does not mean that we do not propose to have a uniform system whereby relief and remedy may be provided for those cases which have been the subject of this debate.
Will it be by legislation or by order in council?
I do not know.
I think it ought to be by legislation.

It will depend upon how we get along. I have heard everyone talking about the War Measures Act, and I have been rather intrigued by what has been said. Generally the War Measures Act is anathema to everyone and we are not supposed to use it, but now everybody is suggesting that we make use of it.

It is a
question of jurisdiction.

The jurisdiction would be under the peace, order and good government provisions of the British North America Act. The War Measures Act gives the government authority to legislate in war time. Which method will be adopted will be considered and announced as soon as possible.

As other speakers have pointed out, I feel that this should be considered a national obligation. I think the hon. member for Saskatoon City (Mr. Bence) covered it very well when he gave the 'details of the legislation that exists in the different provinces. He said that in Saskatchewan provision is made for certain tax deductions. More than that, there is general protection for the soldier for two years after the end of the war or for two years after his discharge. I know something of the dissatisfaction which exists among members of the forces overseas. A chap may come home and hear that one of his pals has received certain protection. He does not know whether he received it under a provincial or a dominion statute. He goes to his municipal officers and asks for similar protection, for the cancellation of taxes in some cases, but it cannot be given.
While we feel sure that the provincial legislatures would be willing to cooperate in doing something to protect these people, the fact is that it is distinctly a national matter. The minister and the government should act to provide legislation to protect these people. There is a great deal in what the hon. member for Lethbridge said. When war was declared many of those who joined the services had just gone through a long period of depression. When they enlisted many of them were carrying liabilities of considerable magnitude. If the interest on these liabilities is to pile up, these men will find on their discharge that they are in a hopeless position. I trust the federal government will take th^ proper means to protect these people and give them the same opportunity after discharge as has been available to those' who continued in civilian life and have had opportunities to pay off their liabilities.
War Appropriation-Army

Last night when we were discussing the Dieppe raid the minister said that he would give me the number of nazi prisoners who had been taken.
I have not that information yet.

Since this subject has now been concluded, there are some questions I should like to ask the minister with a view to ascertaining our man-power situation in so far as the army is concerned. Last evening, as reported at page 3031 of Hansard, the minister set forth the number of "R" recruits accepted and the number of volunteers enlisted in the several military districts. Those facts by themselves do not tell the story complete in detail that the house and the country wish to know.
In the January and February, 1943, issues of "Canada at War" there was a full record of the intake in the armed forces. Early in March I raised a question with regard to this information and analysed it at some length. It may be just a coincidence, but the subsequent issues did not carry any of this information. Therefore it becomes necessary to ask certain questions of the minister in order to bring the record up to date. The first is this: How many men have enlisted in the' army up to the latest available date, which I would take to be April 30?
From the beginning of the war?

Yes. According to the February issue the number up to the end of December was 433,876. Then I should like the numbers of those who have been discharged. We have no information on that beyond the 15th day of February. Next I should like the record showing the enlistments month by month from the 1st of January of this year down to date.
I should also like some information in regard to the operation of the call-up. Page 23 of "Canada at War" indicates that the army asks the department, Labour, I suppose it is to-day, to call up a certain number of men. The army sets 'out its requirements of man-power for the current month. We find that as of December last only 55 [DOT] 7 per cent of those called up from May 15 to December 26 actually found their way into the army.
Are the numbers given there?

The numbers requisitioned, during that period, it states, were

94,000 men, and the number accepted for training was only 52,478. In other words, we were getting a little over fifty per cent of the number of men requisitioned. I should like the minister to explain, in view of the fact that we were getting only about fifty-five per cent of the number of men requisitioned, how it can be said that we were getting the necessary man-power as required. I would point out that in the period from May 20, 1941, to April 9, 1942, -we were getting that manpower as requisitioned for, because the numbers requisitioned under the National Resources Mobilization Act were 56,390 ; 97'9 per cent of the men called up were secured. The figures indicate that the men were not now being secured according to the needs of the military authorities during the period from May 15 to December, 1942, because only 55-7 per cent of those requisitioned were being secured. Why is it that there is no approach at equality of call-up of man-power under the National Resources Mobilization Act? That is a question I have asked on several occasions, but I have not as yet received information thereon.

What does my hon. friend
mean?

I point out this, that according to the figures shown at page 22 of "Canada at War", in the February issue, 1943, there is a complete inequality in the calling up of man-power as between the different military districts. Taking the military districts, when one deducts the numbers who have enlisted from the numbers of the male population aged from nineteen to forty-five years of age who were available at the beginning 'of the war, it will be seen that in military district No. 1, London, up to December 31, 1942, although it had a fine record and a very large percentage of voluntary enlistments, namely 32-3 per cent, 8-52 per cent of the still available man-ipower left over was called up.
Halifax, military district No. 6, had a remarkable record of voluntary enlistments, 39-8 per cent, and yet 10-54 per cent of the still available -man-power was called up under the National Resources Mobilization Act.
Take military district No. 7, Saint John. It had a fine record of voluntary enlistments of 37-2 per cent, and yet we find that 9-89 per cent of the still available man-power was called up under the act.
Take the other districts. Military district No. 4, Montreal, had a record of voluntary enlistments of 16-8 per cent, but only 6-71 per cent were called up under the National Resources Mobilization Act.

War Appropriation-Army
Military district No. 5, Quebec, had an enlistment record of 9-9 per cent, and only 4-59 per cent were called up.
In military district No. 2, Toronto, the callup under N.R.M.A. was 5-82 per cent of the man-power between nineteen and forty-five after deduction of voluntary enlistments; in military district No. 10, Winnipeg, the call-up under N.R.M.A. was 7-22 per cent; in military district' No. 11, Victoria, the call-up was 6-98 per cent; in military district No. 12, Regina, the call-up was 7-69 per cent. I point this out in reference to Saskatchewan, that our record of voluntary enlistments from that province is better than the statistics show, namely 28-6 per cent, for the percentage of enlistments is based on the 1940 population, since when, according to the recent census, about one-fifth of our population has left the province.
I want the minister to explain to the committee and the country why it is there is such an inequality in the percentage of call-ups under the National Resources Mobilization Act.
I wonder if my hon. friend and I are thinking of the same thing. I do not call up; the call is not made by me.
You make the requisition.

I do not requisition from particular districts. I ask for so many men to report at different depots. They can come from British Columbia, Halifax, anywhere at all; I do not designate the district from which they shall come.

Every one of the
ministers says that some other minister is responsible.
I do not think I am one who attempts to shelve responsibility.

No; the minister
does not.
I am asking if my hon. friend suggests that I dictate where the men shall come from?
I do not care who is dictating. I want an explanation from the responsible minister why this condition prevails.
I am only saying my hon. friend cannot get it from me.
All right.

What we do is to make
a requisition or statement showing that we want so many men at such and such a depot.
The men may come to these depots from any place in the dominion. National War Services, and more lately the Department of Labour, through its registrars and boards, decide what men shall be requisitioned.
The minister requisitions the men. The responsibility for the failure to apply equality of call must then rest upon the Minister of National War Services.
Wait till you find whether there is a failure or not. All I say is that the decision as to where the men are to come from does not come from national defence.

I am taking the
record as it appears. I do not know whether it comes under the jurisdiction of the minister, but I should like to know the number of defaulters who have failed to answer the call under N.R.M.A. I think we should have the record of them up to date.
I cannot give my hon. friend that.

Of the three divisions in Canada, would the minister be able to say whether they are up to strength; how many are volunteers available for service anywhere, and how many of them are men called1 up under the National Resources Mobilization Act?	.

I cannot give my hon. friend the strengths of the different divisions. The hon. member for York-Sunbury asked me last nigjjt the number of home defence men, which I intend to give. I can state that, but I am not in a position to give the number in each unit or each formation.
Would the minister give the number of volunteers for service anywhere and those subject only to service in Canada composing the three divisions?

I will put this number on the record now. The hon. member for York-Sunbury asked last night:
How many home defence men are there serving in the Canadian army; that is, men who are not available for service anywhere outside Canada?
As at May 15, 1943, the number of members (H.D.) and "R" recruits serving in the Canadian army was reported at 68,228. These men are of course available for service outside Canada if required under order in council from time to time; and of the number stated, some are actually serving outside Canada, namely, in Newfoundland and on other out* posts and islands.
War Appropriation-Army

I ask these questions at one time so that I shall not be rising too often. What has been the cost of recruiting for the army during the past year? I think that is a figure we should have.
Finally, I should like to make a suggestion with regard to man-power, and to ascertain the attitude of the minister with regard thereto. At the end of January, 1943, there were in the United States 91,800 Canadians, males between eighteen and thirty-eight years of age who are not United States citizens and had not given any indication that they would apply for United States citizenship. There are some five thousand Canadian males serving in the American forces. Under the present arrangements, as I understand' them, between the governments, when a Canadian is called for compulsory service in the United States, an opportunity is given to him to decide whether he will serve in the United States army or in the Canadian army. Having regard to the fact that there are almost one hundred thousand Canadians over there, in the said age limits, and that the total number -who have joined the Canadian army up to the middle of January last was only 801, my question is this, what is being done to secure the availability for service in the Canadian army of those Canadians in the United States who are subject to the National Resources Mobilization Act?
The 90.000 odd whom my hon. friend has mentioned are of all ages, I suppose?

They are males from eighteen to thirty-eight. What has been done to secure these men for the Canadian army? The records I have are that all the enlistments of Canadians in the United States for the Canadian army up to the end of January numbered only 801. Canada established a number of recruiting agencies in the United States and sent Canadian army officers and non-commissioned officers to undertake recruiting, and in the period from the entry of the United States into the war, secured only so few men in that country. I suggest there is a potentially productive field for enlistment there; there must be a large number of men available. I wish to know what is being done to assure their availability, and also what has been and is being done to secure the transfer of Canadians serving in the United States army into the Canadian army for active service.

On this question of the quotas, I quite understand

the procedure. The minister requisitions to the appropriate department-up to a certain period of time the national war service department, now the Department of Labour-for a given number of men. The allotment of these men is the task of, in the first place, the national war service department, and now the labour department.
I do not wish to mislead my hon. friend. I requisitioned for so many men to report at different depots. I do not care where they are drawn from.

I know; the minister assumes no responsibility for that, and I am not finding any fault with that. I am trying to state what I understand the modus operandi to be. That requisition went to the national war service department in the first instance and for a good many months after the National Resources Mobilization Act was in effect. I made inquiry here as to the basis of the allocation of the quotas from each military district, and to my surprise I found that the allocation was based, not at all on the available man-power, but on the record of voluntary enlistments in those districts. That is to say, if New Brunswick and Nova Scotia had a record of thirty-five and thirty-seven per cent, and an adjoining district had a record of ten or thirteen per cent, Nova Scotia or New Brunswick was called upon to contribute two and a half times as many men under the call than the district alongside, whose voluntary enlistments were considerably less.
I think my hon. friend is wrong.

I am not wrong. I was shocked to find that such was the situation. It is not fair. I think I can turn up the report of the discussion in this house. It was not fair then; it is not fair to-day, and there is no equality of sacrifice or service under the method adopted for the man-power policy of this country in respect of the armed forces.
I think my hon. friend wall find, if he looks at the record of the enrolments-and that is what we call them, instead of "enlistments"-that there is no such discrepancy as he has suggested.

I think there is.
